resources.string: Taps the shutter of your camera app on a timer

Lets CAELIS press the shutter button in the camera app you choose, so time-lapse frames keep your camera app\'s full image quality. No screen content is stored or sent anywhere, except the steps of a camera mode you record yourself, kept on this phone.

Brings the chosen camera app to the front when the session starts and then taps its shutter, so every frame keeps that app\'s full quality. Leave the app on screen with the display on: if it goes away, the session pauses until it is back.

After each shot the app checks that a new photo really appeared, and warns you if the camera app stopped saving. To do that it has to read your photo library, which is why Android asks for the photos permission when you switch this on. Leave it off and no photo access is requested at all.

Interval after the photo is finished

The next shot is taken one interval after the previous photo is finished, never during it. For Night Sight and Astro, which take minutes. The end is seen in the photo library when photo access is allowed, otherwise on the camera app’s shutter.

Watches the gyroscope before and during a time-lapse and warns when the phone moves like it is held instead of standing on a tripod. It only warns; shooting carries on. Turn it off for a hyperlapse shot from the hand.

Holds the display awake for as long as the session is actually shooting, because most camera apps stop previewing — and stop taking photos — once the screen goes off. It costs battery and leaves the screen lit for the whole run.

The app taps for you, so Android asks for a few things first. This list is live — come back after each step.

Because this build was installed outside a store, Android blocks its accessibility switch until you unblock it: open App info, tap the menu in the top right corner, choose Allow restricted settings, and confirm. Then come back and enable the service below.
The only way an app can press another app\'s shutter button. Find CAELIS shutter under Installed apps or Downloaded apps and switch it on.
Needed to show the calibration crosshair and the session controls on top of the camera app.
Shows the running session, the shot counter and any warning while the screen is on the camera app.
Without this exemption Android can freeze the app during long sessions and frames go missing.
Intervals of a minute or longer wait on an alarm while the phone sleeps. Without this permission Android may deliver it minutes late. Switch on Alarms & reminders for CAELIS.
Allow CAELIS to use an accessibility service?

CAELIS is not an accessibility tool. It uses Android's accessibility service only to tap the screen for you on a timer: the shutter button in the camera app you choose or, in Periodic tap mode, the spot you calibrated, whatever is on screen.

While the service is on, it sees which app is in the foreground and the layout of that app's screen, so it can find the shutter button and check before every tap that the right app is open and the screen is unlocked. It taps only during a session you started.

Nothing the service sees is stored, logged or sent anywhere. The one exception is a camera mode you record yourself: the positions of your taps and swipes and which buttons of the camera app they hit are kept on this phone, to switch the camera into that mode at the start of a session.

After you agree, Android's accessibility settings open: find CAELIS shutter and switch it on. You can switch it off there at any time.

Augmented reality solar and lunar trajectory and rise/set ephemeris
Draws the terrain skyline in AR and reports when the Sun really goes behind it.
The Sun does not clear the terrain at all today.

The stretch of the trajectory behind the terrain is drawn faint, so you can see how much of the golden hour the hills take.
An elevation tile is 5 to 19 MB, and the peak names for it a few kB more. Elevation comes from AWS, peak names from a public GitHub repository; allowing downloads covers both.
Use the real horizon in Night Sky
Replaces the stylised tree line with the terrain around you, and hides the stars behind it.
Labels the peaks that stand on the skyline with their name and height. Needs the real horizon.

To draw the real skyline, the app needs elevation data for the square of the map you are standing in. Once allowed, data for your current location will be downloaded in the background as needed and cached for offline use; a larger download (over 50 MB by default) waits for your tap. In Settings you can switch to downloading on demand only. Peak names (a few kB per tile) are fetched the same way from a public GitHub repository. Each request carries only the name of that one-degree tile — no coordinates, no identifiers, nothing about you — but the host, like any server you connect to, sees your IP address.\n\nYou can also import the file by hand instead, or change your mind later in Settings.
Off by default. Off means the AR screens use only the phone\'s own sensors, and Google\'s AR component is never started or contacted.
Locks the overlay to the real world through Google\'s Visual Positioning Service. Sends camera-derived data and your location to Google.
Google Play Services for AR comes with this phone\'s system (version %1$s). Nothing needs to be installed.
Google Play Services for AR is installed (version %1$s).
Google Play Services for AR is not installed on this phone, or is disabled. This app does not install it; the AR screens use the phone\'s own sensors.
Allow Google Play Services for AR?

ARCore is not part of this app. It is Google Play Services for AR, a separate component made and run by Google. This app starts it only while an AR screen is open, and only if you allow it here.

While it runs, Google's component may send Google device identifiers, usage data and diagnostics. This app sends nothing itself, and cannot see or limit what Google's component sends. If the component is missing or this phone does not support it, the app does not install it for you and keeps using the phone's own sensors.

While ARCore runs it takes over the camera, so the picture pauses briefly when it starts and when it stops. Zooming past 1x hands the camera back to the app's own camera, and ARCore waits until you are back at 1x.

You can switch it off again at any time in Settings.

The Geospatial API works out where you are by comparing what the camera sees with Google\'s imagery. For that, Google Play Services for AR sends camera-derived visual data and your location to Google\'s Visual Positioning Service, in addition to what ARCore already reports. This app cannot see or limit it.\n\nIt runs only while an AR screen is open. You can switch it off again at any time in Settings.
